metadata.title: Jensen Huang is back as the chief at Nvidia

content.text:
NVIDIA has just announced that it is bringing back Jensen Huang as the CEO of the company, following his resignation earlier this month after a scandalous set of events. The company announced that the board unanimously agreed in favor of bringing back Huang, but the independent investigation will proceed.
"The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company said in an official statement.
The controversy that led to Huang's resignation
Earlier this month, Huang resigned following reports that he had cheated on his wife. Numerous outlets detailed his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an NVIDIA customer that is facing scrutiny over the possible diversion of advanced chips to China. This was followed by separate reports claiming that Huang had romantic relationships with at least two NVIDIA employees.
Soon after his resignation, numerous Silicon Valley executives, including elite figures like Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, voiced their support for bringing back Huang as the chief of NVIDIA, praising his ability to run a company that has been at the vanguard of the current AI boom. Both backed a "Stand with Jensen" petition calling for his reinstatement.
The national security investigation isn't over yet
Now that Huang is back as the CEO of NVIDIA, the board has announced that its independent investigation will continue, including into reports that Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence as part of a honeypot operation involving Alice Huang. The FBI is reportedly looking into the matter, although US President Donald Trump, who said he "would not mind" Huang's return, has publicly questioned claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Meanwhile, the Justice Department and Commerce Department are examining Megaspeed over allegations that it sold chips to China. The scrutiny adds fresh pressure around export rules covering chips and frontier AI technology, at a time when the US and China are locked in a white-hot race for AI supremacy.
